title: The Busiest Traders Earned the Least

beats.text: The investors who worked hardest at the stock market earned the least.
Imagine it's the early nineties. You're Dave, calling your broker every week.
Buy this, sell that. Your portfolio turns over more than twice a year.
Your neighbor Pat barely touches the phone.
Two professors studied sixty-six thousand households like yours.
The market returned seventeen point nine percent a year.
The busiest traders? Eleven point four.
So where did the money go?
You see, trading is a highway with a toll booth at every exit.
Each round trip cost about four percent in commissions and spreads.
Before the tolls, Dave kept pace with the market.
And Pat, who barely traded? Eighteen and a half percent.
The market never beat Dave. His phone did.

facts.claim: Barber & Odean studied 66,465 households with accounts at a large discount broker, 1991 to 1996 (Journal of Finance, 2000)
The market returned 17.9 percent a year; the households that traded most earned 11.4 percent net; the average household 16.4 percent
The households that traded most turned over more than 250 percent of their portfolio a year (more than twice a year)
The average round-trip trade above $1,000 cost about 3 percent in commissions and 1 percent in bid-ask spread (about four percent)
Gross (before-cost) returns of frequent and infrequent traders were close to the market; the gap came from trading costs, not stock picks
Infrequent traders earned 18.5 percent a year net
Dave and Pat are fictional illustrations of the study's most-active and least-active households

caption:
66,465 households. Six years of real trades.
The busiest traders earned 11.4% a year while the market made 17.9%.
Their picks weren't the problem. The tolls were.
